c.tagline: Seljuk Anatolia at the foot of Mount Erciyes — pastırma, citadel bazaars and the road to Cappadocia.

taxi.fareNote: Taxis are metered; hailing via the BiTaksi app (or Uber, which dispatches licensed taxis) avoids fare disputes.

emergency.note: 112 is Türkiye's single emergency number for ambulance, fire and police.

hood_desc: The historic core around Cumhuriyet Square, dominated by the black-stone Kayseri Castle, the covered bazaar and Seljuk monuments like the Hunat Hatun Complex; the best base for sightseeing on foot.
The main central district spreading south and east of the old city, with modern shopping, parks, hotels and Erciyes University nearby; a convenient, well-connected place to stay.
The western central district around the railway station and business areas, with malls and the Kayseray tram running through; practical and well-served by transit.
A historic hillside town, now a leafy university suburb east of the center, known for restored stone houses, cafés and cooler air; a relaxed, characterful alternative to the city center.
A village-like neighborhood on the lower slopes of Mount Erciyes, the gateway to the Erciyes ski resort; quiet and scenic, best for skiers and mountain trips.

water.note: Tap is treated but most locals drink bottled water.

transit.hours: The Kayseray tram and city buses run roughly 6:00 AM to midnight; taxis and ride apps cover later hours.
transit.note: Kayseri's public transport centers on the Kayseray light-rail tram line crossing the city, backed by an extensive municipal bus network; a single Kart 38 smartcard works across both.
transit.pay: Tram and buses are cashless — you tap a rechargeable Kart 38 smartcard, sold and topped up at stations and kiosks; single fares are inexpensive.

bus: Kayseri Intercity Bus Terminal (regional & national coaches)

transit.m: City bus to the center (~25-30 min)
Taxi to the city center (10-15 min)

tip.r: Around 5-10% at restaurants is customary for good service; leaving it in cash is preferred.

food.name: Kayseri mantisi
food.desc: Thumbnail-sized meat dumplings, famously small enough that forty should fit on a spoon, drowned in garlic yoghurt, chilli butter and sumac.

places.name: Elmacioglu Iskender
places.note: The best-known address in town for classic Kayseri manti, going strong for decades.

places.name: Kasik-la
places.note: Kayseri-cuisine specialist praised in recent reviews for its manti and yaglama.

places.name: Sultan Sofrasi
places.note: Home-style kitchen where manti sits alongside the rest of the regional repertoire.

food.name: Pastirma
food.desc: Air-dried beef crusted in cemen, a paste of fenugreek, garlic and paprika; Kayseri's most famous export, sliced paper thin.

places.name: Pastirmacilar Carsisi
places.note: The pastirma traders' bazaar itself, where shops cure and slice to order.

places.name: Basyazici Et Lokantasi
places.note: Meat house recommended locally for pastirma and sucuk served hot rather than as deli slices.

places.name: Kasik-la
places.note: Its serpme Kayseri breakfast puts pastirma next to kaymak and honey.

food.name: Kayseri sucugu
food.desc: Firm, garlicky cured beef sausage heavy with cumin and red pepper, fried until the fat runs and eaten with eggs or in pide.

places.name: Basyazici Et Lokantasi
places.note: Go-to for sucuk cooked in the pan, from a kitchen built around Kayseri charcuterie.

places.name: Kapali Carsi butchers
places.note: Covered-bazaar makers sell vacuum-packed rings that travel home well.

places.name: Sultan Sofrasi
places.note: Sucuklu yumurta and sucuklu pide on a menu of everyday Kayseri cooking.

food.name: Yaglama
food.desc: Stacked layers of thin yufka bread brushed with spiced minced-meat sauce and yoghurt, cut in wedges like a savoury Anatolian cake.

places.name: Sultan Sofrasi
places.note: Named by local guides as an ideal spot for yaglama and other regional plates.

places.name: Kasik-la
places.note: Reviewers single out the yaglama here alongside the manti.

places.name: Elmacioglu Iskender
places.note: Serves yaglama as part of the traditional Kayseri spread.

food.name: Pastirmali pide
food.desc: Boat-shaped flatbread baked with pastirma, cheese and egg so the cemen crust perfumes the whole thing; the city's favourite quick lunch.

places.name: Kapali Carsi pide ovens
places.note: Wood-fired ovens around the covered bazaar bake to order for market crowds.

places.name: Basyazici Et Lokantasi
places.note: Uses its own cured meat, so the pastirma layer is unusually generous.

places.name: Sultan Sofrasi
places.note: Dependable pide list for a fast, cheap sit-down meal in the centre.

food.name: Nevzine tatlisi
food.desc: Kayseri's own sherbet-soaked pastry, a dense nut-filled square cut in diamonds and served with clotted cream at celebrations.

places.name: Kapali Carsi sweet shops
places.note: Traditional tatlici counters in the bazaar keep trays of nevzine and unnabi.

places.name: Sultan Sofrasi
places.note: Regional desserts follow the meal, nevzine among them when in season.

places.name: Cumhuriyet Meydani pastry shops
places.note: Cluster of pastanes on the main square selling boxed nevzine to take away.

food.name: Gilaburu juice
food.desc: Fiercely sour juice pressed from guelder-rose berries grown around Kayseri, drunk cold with a little honey and credited with all sorts of cures.

places.name: Kapali Carsi juice stalls
places.note: Bazaar sellers press it fresh and sell bottles of the local berry harvest.

places.name: Sultan Sofrasi
places.note: Keeps gilaburu on the drinks list beside ayran and turnip juice.

places.name: Pastirmacilar Carsisi shops
places.note: Sold alongside pastirma and molasses as a Kayseri regional product.

food.name: Ayran
food.desc: Whipped salted yoghurt drink served frothy and ice cold; the standard cut-through for pastirma fat and chilli butter on manti.

places.name: Elmacioglu Iskender
places.note: Poured by the glass with every plate of manti and iskender.

places.name: Basyazici Et Lokantasi
places.note: Churned ayran that stands up to a heavy meat lunch.

places.name: Kapali Carsi kiosks
places.note: Cheap cups from bazaar kiosks, best with a pastirmali pide in hand.

landmarks: Kayseri Castle (Kayseri Kalesi)
Massive black volcanic-stone walls begun by Byzantine emperor Justinian and rebuilt by Seljuks dominate the city centre, now enclosing a cultural and shopping precinct.
Mount Erciyes
This snow-capped 3,917-metre extinct volcano looms over the city skyline, luring skiers in winter and hikers in summer to Anatolia's rooftop.
Hunat Hatun Complex
A superb 13th-century Seljuk ensemble of mosque, madrasa, tomb and bathhouse built for a sultan's wife, showcasing Kayseri's golden medieval age.
Grand Mosque (Ulu Cami)
Founded by the Danishmend dynasty in the 12th century, this forest of ancient columns remains one of Anatolia's oldest continuously used mosques.
Döner Kümbet
A beautifully carved cylindrical Seljuk tomb tower from 1276, its twelve-sided stone drum and conical roof form Kayseri's most elegant funerary monument.
Kayseri Covered Bazaar and Vezirhan
One of Turkey's largest historic bazaars, trading since Ottoman times in pastırma, sucuk and carpets beneath centuries-old vaulted stone ceilings.
Seljuk Civilization Museum (Gevher Nesibe Darüşşifa)
The world's first medical school and hospital, built in 1206 for a Seljuk princess, now houses an engaging museum of Seljuk science and art.
Kültepe (Kanesh) Archaeological Site
A short drive away lies the Bronze Age trading colony where Anatolia's earliest written records emerged, a 4,000-year-old Assyrian merchant city.
Kayseri Archaeology Museum
Cuneiform tablets from Kültepe, Hittite lions and Roman treasures chart six millennia of Cappadocian history in this rewarding modern collection.
Soğanlı Valley
A day-trip-able Cappadocian valley of rock-cut Byzantine churches with faded frescoes, far quieter than Göreme yet just as hauntingly beautiful.

train.note: No international trains. Kayseri is on the main line east from Ankara, with conventional services including the Doğu Ekspresi to Kars and trains toward Adana and Divriği; a YHT high-speed link to Ankara and Sivas is being built. Book on TCDD e-bilet from 15 days out - the scenic Doğu Ekspresi sells out weeks ahead in winter.

bus.note: No international coaches. Kayseri's terminal is a gateway to Cappadocia, with frequent minibuses and coaches to Göreme and Ürgüp (about 1h15) as well as Metro Turizm (https://www.metroturizm.com.tr/en) and Süha services to Ankara, Istanbul and Adana. Book through obilet (https://www.obilet.com/en/); many Cappadocia hotels also run airport and otogar shuttles.

ferry.note: Kayseri is inland in central Anatolia beneath Mount Erciyes, with no coast or navigable water, so there are no ferries.

half.name: Göreme
half.blurb: Cave churches carved into cone-shaped volcanic rock formations, some painted with Byzantine frescoes, are clustered in this Cappadocia valley.

half.name: Ürgüp
half.blurb: Rock-cut cave dwellings and underground wine cellars sit beneath fairy chimney formations in this Cappadocia town.

half.name: Sultan Marshes
half.blurb: A wetland reserve fed by two lakes attracts flamingos, cranes, and other migratory birds across its reed beds and salt flats.
